pos: n. (archaic; the condition of being ill-favoured, deformity, anything unseemly in an offering)
etymology: A compound of evil and favoured, the latter from Old French faveur, countenance or appearance. To be ill-favoured is to be of bad appearance. The Hebrew phrase is dabar ra, an evil thing or bad matter in the beast.
biblical_def: The law of the offering admits no defective animal: “Thou shalt not sacrifice unto the LORD thy God any bullock, or sheep, wherein is blemish, or any evilfavouredness: for that is an abomination unto the LORD thy God” (Deuteronomy 17:1). Evilfavouredness is the widest word in the Authorized Version for the unseemly. The law has already named particular blemishes elsewhere; this clause closes the gap by forbidding anything ill-favoured whatever, any defect a worshipper might think too slight to matter or too vague to be listed. And the verdict is not that such an offering is inadequate but that it is an abomination, the strongest word in the covenant vocabulary. Leviticus says the same from the positive side: “But whatsoever hath a blemish, that shall ye not offer: for it shall not be acceptable for you” (Leviticus 22:20). Malachi shows what became of the law in practice, when priests brought the blind and the lame and God sent them to try it on the governor first (Malachi 1:8). All of it was pointing forward. The offering God accepted was a Lamb without blemish and without spot, whose body was prepared for Him and in whom no fault was found.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): ILL-FAVORED, ugly; of bad appearance; EVIL-FAVOREDNESS, deformity; any thing unseemly.
webster_full: EVIL-FAVOREDNESS, n. Deformity; any thing unseemly or of bad appearance.
ILL-FAVORED, a. Ugly; of a bad countenance or appearance.
FAVOR, n. Countenance; appearance; the look or aspect of a thing.
Hebrew dabar ra, an evil thing or bad matter found in the beast.
Deuteronomy 17:1 forbids offering any bullock or sheep wherein is evilfavouredness.
scriptures: Deu 17:1
Thou shalt not sacrifice unto the LORD thy God any bullock, or sheep, wherein is blemish, or any evilfavouredness: for that is an abomination unto the LORD thy God.
But whatsoever hath a blemish, that shall ye not offer: for it shall not be acceptable for you.
Mal 1:8

And if ye offer the blind for sacrifice, is it not evil? and if ye offer the lame and sick, is it not evil? offer it now unto thy governor; will he be pleased with thee, or accept thy person? saith the LORD of hosts.
corruption_summary: Worship is judged by the worshipper's sincerity rather than by God's stated requirement, so that a defective offering is excused as long as the heart meant well.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern instinct is that God looks at the heart, and therefore that the quality of what is brought cannot matter much. Sincerity becomes the whole of acceptability. On that account evilfavouredness is a ceremonial technicality long since outgrown, and the priests of Malachi's day were guilty of nothing worse than being under-resourced.

God does look at the heart, which is precisely why He rejects the blemished offering: the man who keeps the sound beast and brings the lame one has told the truth about his heart. Malachi's test exposes it, for the same man would not insult his governor with such a gift. The principle carries straight into the regulative principle of worship. God, not the worshipper, says what He will receive; and under the gospel the acceptable offering is not our best beast but a Lamb without blemish, in whom alone our worship is received.

pos: adj. (of flint; hard as flint, unyielding)
etymology: From flint, Old English flint, a hard quartz stone that strikes fire. The Hebrew in Deuteronomy 32:13 is chalmish, flint or hardest rock.
biblical_def: The song of Moses recounts the LORD's dealings with Jacob in the wilderness: “He made him ride on the high places of the earth, that he might eat the increase of the fields; and he made him to suck honey out of the rock, and oil out of the flinty rock” (Deuteronomy 32:13). Flinty means of flint, the hardest and least promising stone in the land, which yields nothing to a man's hand but sparks. From that rock God drew oil, as from the rock He had drawn water in a place of drought: “who brought thee forth water out of the rock of flint” (Deuteronomy 8:15). The theology of the whole song is in that image. Israel's provision never came from the fertility of the circumstances; it came from the LORD, who is Himself called the Rock in this same chapter, and who makes the barren place a table. Asaph presses the same figure as a lament over what unbelief forfeited: “with honey out of the rock should I have satisfied thee” (Psalm 81:16). The flinty rock is therefore the standing proof that God's people are never limited by the soil they stand on.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): FLINTY, consisting of flint; like flint; very hard; cruel; unmerciful; inexorable.
webster_full: FLINTY, a. Consisting of flint; as a flinty rock.
Like flint; very hard; not impressible; as a flinty heart.
Cruel; unmerciful; inexorable.
FLINT, n. A sub-species of quartz, of a yellowish or blackish gray, which strikes fire with steel.
Deuteronomy 32:13 says God drew oil out of the flinty rock.
scriptures: He made him ride on the high places of the earth, that he might eat the increase of the fields; and he made him to suck honey out of the rock, and oil out of the flinty rock;
Deu 8:15
Who led thee through that great and terrible wilderness, wherein were fiery serpents, and scorpions, and drought, where there was no water; who brought thee forth water out of the rock of flint;
He should have fed them also with the finest of the wheat: and with honey out of the rock should I have satisfied thee.
corruption_summary: The wilderness provisions are explained away as folk memory of ordinary desert resourcefulness, emptying the song of Moses of the God who gives from stone.
corruption_paragraphs: A standard modern treatment turns the honey and oil from the flinty rock into a poetic memory of bees nesting in clefts and olive trees rooted in limestone: nothing supernatural, only a people making the most of hard country. The reading is not offered as an addition to the text but as a replacement for it, and it travels with the wider claim that the Song of Moses is a late composition retrojected onto the wilderness.

The dictionary holds Mosaic authorship and the plain historical sense. Moses names the LORD as the agent in every clause: He made him ride, He made him to suck honey out of the rock. The point of a flinty rock is precisely that it cannot be made to yield; the miracle is the doctrine. And the pastoral use follows directly: the believer in hard country is not told to find hidden resources in the stone, but to look to the Rock that gave Israel oil.

pos: n. (depth; the quality of being deep, here of soil)
etymology: From deep, Old English deop, with the noun-forming suffix -ness. The Greek is bathos, depth, the word behind English bathos and bathymetry.
biblical_def: In the parable of the sower the second soil is defined by what it lacks: “Some fell upon stony places, where they had not much earth: and forthwith they sprung up, because they had no deepness of earth” (Matthew 13:5). Deepness is depth, and the whole diagnosis of the second hearer lies in that one noun. The stony ground is not cold ground. It is the quickest of the four, springing up forthwith, before the good soil has shown anything at all. What it has not got is depth, and so it has no root; and when the sun rises the speed that looked like life is exposed: “And when the sun was up, they were scorched; and because they had no root, they withered away” (Matthew 13:6). Our Lord gives the interpretation Himself: “Yet hath he not root in himself, but dureth for a while: for when tribulation or persecution ariseth because of the word, by and by he is offended” (Matthew 13:21). The parable therefore warns against measuring a work of grace by its first enthusiasm. Rapid response proves nothing; root proves everything, and root is a work only God gives.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): DEEPNESS, entrance far below the surface; depth; profundity.
webster_full: DEEPNESS, n. Entrance far below the surface; the distance or extent to which any thing reaches downward; depth.
Craft; insidiousness. (a secondary and now obsolete sense)
Greek bathos, depth.
Matthew 13:5 says the stony ground had no deepness of earth.
Mark 4:5 renders the same clause depth of earth.
scriptures: Mat 13:5
Some fell upon stony places, where they had not much earth: and forthwith they sprung up, because they had no deepness of earth:
Mat 13:6
And when the sun was up, they were scorched; and because they had no root, they withered away.
Yet hath he not root in himself, but dureth for a while: for when tribulation or persecution ariseth because of the word, by and by he is offended.
corruption_summary: Immediate emotional response to preaching is counted as conversion, so that the stony ground is routinely reported as fruit and the absence of root is discovered only when trouble comes.
corruption_paragraphs: Revivalist and seeker-driven methods have made the stony-ground response the measure of success. Hands raised, decisions counted, a visible surge of joy; and the surge is published as harvest. Our Lord says that this soil is the quickest of all and bears nothing. The method that optimises for speed of response is optimising for exactly the ground He warns about.

The remedy is not coldness in preaching but a right doctrine of regeneration. Root is not produced by the hearer's decision; it is given with a new heart, and it shows itself in perseverance when tribulation ariseth. Hence the Reformed insistence that perseverance is the fruit of genuine regeneration rather than a second blessing added to it, and the pastoral practice of patient catechesis in place of counting hands.

roots_lines: Old English deop, deep, with the suffix -ness.

pos: n. (the state of being green; vigour of growth, freshness)
etymology: From green, Old English grene, akin to grow, with the suffix -ness. The Hebrew ib denotes freshness or greenness in a plant.
biblical_def: Bildad presses the figure of the rush that grows in water and dies when the water fails: “Whilst it is yet in his greenness, and not cut down, it withereth before any other herb” (Job 8:12). Greenness is the vigour of a plant at its freshest. The point of the verse is the speed of the collapse: no sickle touches this rush and no season turns against it, yet it withers first of all the herbs, because its whole life depended on a supply that was never its own. Bildad applies it exactly: “So are the paths of all that forget God; and the hypocrite's hope shall perish” (Job 8:13). The observation is true even though Bildad misapplies it to Job, and Scripture elsewhere confirms it. The man who forgets God may flourish in full greenness and be cut off without a blow, because nothing feeds him. Set against the rush is the tree of the first Psalm: “And he shall be like a tree planted by the rivers of water, that bringeth forth his fruit in his season; his leaf also shall not wither” (Psalm 1:3). Greenness proves nothing; the river proves everything.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): GREENNESS, the quality of being green; viridity; immaturity; freshness; vigor.
webster_full: GREENNESS, n. The quality of being green; viridity; as the greenness of grass.
Immaturity; unripeness; as the greenness of fruit.
Freshness; vigor; newness.
Hebrew ib, freshness or greenness in a plant.

corruption_summary: Visible flourishing is treated as the evidence of God's favour, so that greenness is mistaken for life and the hidden question of the water supply is never asked.
corruption_paragraphs: Prosperity preaching makes greenness the proof. Growth, increase, visible vigour in a life or a ministry are read as God's endorsement, and withering is read as a failure of faith. Bildad's rush answers the first half of that and Job's whole book answers the second: the rush is at its greenest just before it dies, and Job is withered while righteous.

The Scripture asks a different question than the one prosperity teaching asks. Not how green, but what feeds it. The tree of Psalm 1 is planted by the rivers of water, and its leaf does not wither because the supply is not in itself. So the believer is not taught to measure his standing by his present vigour, nor to despair in his present barrenness, but to be planted where the water is: in the law of the LORD, in Christ, in the means of grace.

pos: n. (comeliness, beauty, the attractive excellence of a thing)
etymology: From goodly, Old English godlic, of good appearance, with the suffix -ness. The Hebrew chesed here is used in its rarer sense of comeliness or loveliness rather than covenant mercy.
biblical_def: The voice that commissions Isaiah 40 commands a cry, and the cry begins with the frailty of man: “The voice said, Cry. And he said, What shall I cry? All flesh is grass, and all the goodliness thereof is as the flower of the field” (Isaiah 40:6). Goodliness is comeliness, the attractive excellence of a thing: strength, beauty, standing, talent, every quality that makes a man admired. The prophet does not call it worthless; he calls it a flower. A flower is genuinely beautiful and genuinely brief. And over against it the verse sets the one permanence: “The grass withereth, the flower fadeth: but the word of our God shall stand for ever” (Isaiah 40:8). Peter quotes the passage to a scattered church to tell them where their new birth came from: “For all flesh is as grass, and all the glory of man as the flower of grass” (1 Peter 1:24), and then names the incorruptible seed of the word of God. The word is therefore the hinge of the whole comfort of Isaiah 40. All that Israel admired in Babylon would fade; the word that promised her return would not.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): GOODLINESS, beauty of form; grace; elegance; comeliness.
webster_full: GOODLINESS, n. Beauty of form; grace; elegance; comeliness.
GOODLY, a. Being of a handsome form; beautiful; graceful.
Pleasant; agreeable; desirable.
Hebrew chesed, here in the sense of comeliness or loveliness.

Isa 40:8

For all flesh is as grass, and all the glory of man as the flower of grass. The grass withereth, and the flower thereof falleth away:
corruption_summary: Human excellence is made the measure of a life's worth, and the honest reckoning with its brevity is avoided as morbid rather than received as the beginning of comfort.
corruption_paragraphs: A culture organised around achievement, image and self-realisation cannot hear Isaiah 40:6 as comfort. All flesh is grass sounds like an insult to the project, and so the verse is either avoided or softened into a reminder to live fully in the present. The goodliness of flesh is defended as the very thing worth building a life on.

Isaiah is not being bleak; he is clearing ground. The prophet announces comfort to Jerusalem in the same chapter, and the reason the comfort holds is that it rests on the word of God rather than on anything in man. Peter uses the passage precisely to establish assurance: the believer is born again not of corruptible seed but by the word which liveth and abideth for ever. The honest reckoning with the flower of the field is the doorway to the only hope that does not fade.

pos: adj. (not ripe; not brought to maturity, immature)
etymology: From un- and ripe, Old English ripe, ready for reaping. The Hebrew boser is the sour, unformed grape, the same word behind the sour grapes of the proverb in Jeremiah and Ezekiel.
biblical_def: Eliphaz describes the end of the wicked man in the language of a failed vintage: “He shall shake off his unripe grape as the vine, and shall cast off his flower as the olive” (Job 15:33). An unripe grape is the boser, the hard sour cluster that never came to sweetness, and a vine that sheds such fruit has laboured a whole season for nothing. The olive casting its blossom is the same loss earlier in the cycle. Eliphaz's doctrine is that the wicked man's whole life is a harvest that does not arrive: “For the congregation of hypocrites shall be desolate, and fire shall consume the tabernacles of bribery” (Job 15:34). As a general truth about ungodliness the observation stands, and the dictionary receives it as such; where Eliphaz errs is in turning it into a universal rule by which Job's suffering must prove Job's wickedness. Scripture elsewhere takes up the figure of premature fruit in judgment: the stars fall as a fig tree casteth her untimely figs when shaken of a mighty wind. The unripe grape is thus the standing emblem of a life that had every advantage of vine and season and still came to nothing.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): UNRIPE, not mature; not brought to perfection; not seasonable; too early.
webster_full: UNRIPE, a. Not mature; not brought to a perfect state; as unripe fruit.
Not seasonable; not yet fit; as unripe measures.
RIPE, a. Brought to perfection in growth; mature; fit for reaping.
Hebrew boser, the sour unformed grape.
Job 15:33 says the wicked shall shake off his unripe grape as the vine.
scriptures: He shall shake off his unripe grape as the vine, and shall cast off his flower as the olive.

corruption_summary: Eliphaz's true general observation is hardened into a rule that suffering always proves sin, which is precisely the counsel God rebukes at the end of the book.
corruption_paragraphs: There are two opposite errors around this verse. The first is the error of Job's friends, who took a sound general truth about the barrenness of wickedness and applied it as a diagnostic to a righteous sufferer. The LORD's closing verdict is that they had not spoken of Him the thing that was right. The second error is to dismiss the comforters' speeches wholesale as merely bad theology, which flattens the book and loses the real warnings they contain.

Read rightly, Job 15:33 is a warning to the ungodly and no measuring rod for the afflicted saint. The wicked man's vintage fails; that is true. It does not follow that every failed vintage marks a wicked man, and the sufferer who hears his own barren season in this verse should be sent not to self-accusation but to the tree planted by the rivers of water, whose fruit comes in its season.

pos: v. (past participle of mow; cut down, as grass with a scythe)
etymology: Past participle of mow, Old English mawan, to cut down grass or grain. The Hebrew gez in Psalm 72:6 denotes mown grass or a fleece, that which has been shorn.
biblical_def: The seventy-second Psalm prays for the reign of Solomon and prophesies the reign of Christ: “He shall come down like rain upon the mown grass: as showers that water the earth” (Psalm 72:6). Mown grass is grass already cut, and the image is more tender than it first appears. A mown field is at its most exposed: the covering is gone, the roots are bared to the sun, and nothing but rain will bring it back. Into that condition the King comes, not as heat but as showers. The verse therefore describes the character of Christ's rule before it describes its extent. He comes to a people shorn and does not finish the cutting; He waters it. The next verse gives the result: “In his days shall the righteous flourish; and abundance of peace so long as the moon endureth” (Psalm 72:7). Moses had used the same figure of true doctrine: “My doctrine shall drop as the rain, my speech shall distil as the dew, as the small rain upon the tender herb” (Deuteronomy 32:2). A bruised and mown people is exactly the ground the King chooses to come down upon.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): MOW, to cut down with a scythe, as grass; MOWN, the past participle, cut down.
webster_full: MOW, v.t. To cut down with a scythe, as grass or other plants.
To cut the grass from; as, to mow a meadow.
MOWN, pp. Cut down with a scythe.
Hebrew gez, mown grass or a shorn fleece.

Deu 32:2

corruption_summary: The messianic Psalms are reduced to court poetry for an Israelite king, so that Psalm 72 flatters a monarch instead of promising Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: The dominant academic reading treats Psalm 72 as royal ideology: an enthronement liturgy whose extravagant language about dominion from sea to sea is conventional flattery addressed to a Judean king. On that account the psalm has no prophetic reference at all, and the mown grass is a pleasant agricultural simile for good government.

The New Testament and the whole Reformed tradition read it as Scripture reads itself. No Israelite king ruled from sea to sea, none endured so long as the moon, and none had all nations call him blessed; the psalm closes by naming the LORD God of Israel who only doeth wondrous things. Christ is the King here, and the mown grass is His people. Lose the prophetic reference and the verse loses the comfort it exists to give: that the King comes down as rain upon exactly those who have been cut.

pos: v. (to cut off the top or branches of; to prune away)
etymology: Of uncertain origin, perhaps from Middle English loppe, a branch cut off. To lop is to cut away the upper or outer growth. The Hebrew saaph means to lop off boughs.
biblical_def: Isaiah ends his oracle against Assyrian pride with the LORD among the trees: “Behold, the Lord, the LORD of hosts, shall lop the bough with terror: and the high ones of stature shall be hewn down, and the haughty shall be humbled” (Isaiah 10:33). To lop is to cut off the high growth, and the verb is chosen for the height it removes. God does not uproot the forest here; He takes the tops. The high ones of stature are the proud, and the whole burden of the chapter is that Assyria was an axe in God's hand which boasted as though it swung itself. The prophet's announcement governs every age: “For the day of the LORD of hosts shall be upon every one that is proud and lofty, and upon every one that is lifted up; and he shall be brought low” (Isaiah 2:12). Mary sings the same doctrine in the Magnificat: “He hath put down the mighty from their seats, and exalted them of low degree” (Luke 1:52). The lopping is terrible and it is also merciful, for the next verse of Isaiah brings forth the rod out of the stem of Jesse: what God lops from the proud He raises in His Son.

webster_full: LOP, v.t. To cut off the top or extreme part of any thing; to shorten by cutting off the extremities.
To cut partly off and let hang.
LOP, n. That which is cut from trees.
Hebrew saaph, to lop off boughs.
Isaiah 10:33 says the LORD of hosts shall lop the bough with terror.
scriptures: Behold, the Lord, the LORD of hosts, shall lop the bough with terror: and the high ones of stature shall be hewn down, and the haughty shall be humbled.

corruption_summary: God's humbling of the proud is recast as impersonal historical justice, a long arc that bends on its own, with no Lord of hosts lifting the axe.
corruption_paragraphs: It is easy to agree that the mighty fall. Secular readings of history, and a good deal of political preaching on every side, treat that as a law of systems: empires overreach, power corrodes, the arc bends. The agent disappears. On that account Isaiah 10:33 is an ancient way of saying what sociology now says better.

Isaiah names the agent three times in one clause: Behold, the Lord, the LORD of hosts, shall lop the bough. The Magnificat keeps the same grammar, and keeps it personal: He hath put down the mighty from their seats. This matters pastorally, because an impersonal arc offers no refuge and makes no promise. The God who lops the high ones is the God who brings the rod out of the stem of Jesse, and the humbling and the exalting are the work of the same hand.

pos: v. (to make soft or pliant; here, to cleanse and soften a newborn with water)
etymology: From Old French souple, pliant, from Latin supplex, bending, submissive. As a verb, to supple is to make soft. The Hebrew mishi is a washing or cleansing.
biblical_def: Ezekiel 16 begins with the LORD describing Jerusalem as a newborn abandoned at birth: “And as for thy nativity, in the day thou wast born thy navel was not cut, neither wast thou washed in water to supple thee; thou wast not salted at all, nor swaddled at all” (Ezekiel 16:4). To supple is to make soft and pliant, and it names one of the ordinary offices of care given to an infant: the washing that cleanses and softens the skin. The verse lists four such offices and says that none of them was performed. The cord uncut, the body unwashed, unsalted, unswaddled; a child left in the open field to die. That is the LORD's picture of what Israel was when He found her, and the point is not merely her misery but her total inability. Then comes the word that makes the chapter gospel: “I said unto thee when thou wast in thy blood, Live” (Ezekiel 16:6). God does not find a promising infant; He commands life over a dying one. And having given life, He enters covenant: “I sware unto thee, and entered into a covenant with thee, saith the Lord GOD, and thou becamest mine” (Ezekiel 16:8).
webster_summary: Webster (1828): SUPPLE, to make soft, pliant or flexible; SUPPLE, a. pliant; flexible; yielding.
webster_full: SUPPLE, v.t. To make soft, pliant or flexible; as, to supple leather.
To make compliant; to make submissive.
SUPPLE, a. Pliant; flexible; easily bent; yielding.
From Latin supplex, bending, submissive.
Ezekiel 16:4 says Jerusalem was not washed in water to supple her.
scriptures: Eze 16:4
And as for thy nativity, in the day thou wast born thy navel was not cut, neither wast thou washed in water to supple thee; thou wast not salted at all, nor swaddled at all.
Eze 16:6
And when I passed by thee, and saw thee polluted in thine own blood, I said unto thee when thou wast in thy blood, Live; yea, I said unto thee when thou wast in thy blood, Live.
Eze 16:8

Now when I passed by thee, and looked upon thee, behold, thy time was the time of love; and I spread my skirt over thee, and covered thy nakedness: yea, I sware unto thee, and entered into a covenant with thee, saith the Lord GOD, and thou becamest mine.
corruption_summary: Ezekiel 16 is read as divine harshness toward a woman, and the infant's helplessness is softened into mere disadvantage rather than the death out of which God speaks life.
corruption_paragraphs: Ezekiel 16 is one of the chapters most frequently indicted by progressive commentators, who read the marriage and adultery imagery as a sanctified picture of domination and object to the LORD's language about the unfaithful wife. The chapter is severe, and the dictionary does not soften it; but the indictment misreads the genre and misses the gift. The figure is covenant, not private cruelty, and the one bringing the charge is the one who saved the child in the field.

Lose the helplessness of verse 4 and the whole chapter collapses. An infant with the cord uncut and the body unwashed is not disadvantaged; she is dying, and she contributes nothing to her own rescue. That is unconditional election and effectual calling in narrative form: God passes by, sees a child polluted in her own blood, and says Live. Every later charge of unfaithfulness in the chapter is weighed against that beginning, and so is every mercy promised at its end.
roots_summary: Latin supplex, pliant; Hebrew mishi, a cleansing; Ezekiel 16:4 lists the washing Jerusalem never received.
roots_lines: Old French souple, from Latin supplex, bending or pliant.
Hebrew mishi, a washing or cleansing.
Ezekiel 16:4 is the only occurrence of supple as a verb in the Authorized Version.
Four offices of infant care are named and all four denied.
Ezekiel 16:6 answers the helplessness with the command Live.

names the newborn's washing that Jerusalem never received
sets total inability under the sovereign command Live

pos: v. (past participle; softened, soothed with ointment)
etymology: From Latin mollificare, to make soft, from mollis (soft) and facere (to make). The Hebrew rakak means to be soft or tender, here of a sore softened with oil.
biblical_def: Isaiah opens his prophecy with the nation examined as a body covered in untreated wounds: “From the sole of the foot even unto the head there is no soundness in it; but wounds, and bruises, and putrifying sores: they have not been closed, neither bound up, neither mollified with ointment” (Isaiah 1:6). To mollify is to soften with oil, and the clause names the third of three neglected treatments: the wound not closed, not bound up, not softened with ointment. The sores are not merely present; they are untended, which is the prophet's whole point. Judah had priests, sacrifices, feasts and a temple, and still no one was treating the disease. The preceding verse asks why they should be stricken any more, since “the whole head is sick, and the whole heart faint” (Isaiah 1:5). What the nation needed was not more chastening but a physician. The Samaritan in the parable does exactly what Judah's shepherds would not: he “bound up his wounds, pouring in oil and wine” (Luke 10:34). Isaiah's diagnosis therefore stands as the classic Scriptural statement of total depravity, from the sole of the foot to the head, and as the classic demand for a Saviour who heals rather than merely denounces.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): MOLLIFY, to soften; to make soft or tender; to assuage; to appease.
webster_full: MOLLIFY, v.t. To soften; to make soft or tender.
To assuage, as pain or irritation.
To appease; to pacify; to calm or quiet.
From Latin mollis, soft, and facio, to make.
Isaiah 1:6 says Judah's sores were neither closed, bound up, nor mollified with ointment.
scriptures: Isa 1:6
From the sole of the foot even unto the head there is no soundness in it; but wounds, and bruises, and putrifying sores: they have not been closed, neither bound up, neither mollified with ointment.
Isa 1:5
Why should ye be stricken any more? ye will revolt more and more: the whole head is sick, and the whole heart faint.
And went to him, and bound up his wounds, pouring in oil and wine, and set him on his own beast, and brought him to an inn, and took care of him.
corruption_summary: Sin is treated as sickness in a sense that removes guilt, so that the ointment is applied and the repentance Isaiah demands in the same chapter is never required.
corruption_paragraphs: Isaiah 1:6 is a favourite text of a therapeutic preaching that is glad to speak of wounds, soothing and healing and reluctant to speak of revolt. On that reading the nation is wounded rather than guilty, and what it needs is care rather than conversion. The verse certainly supplies the medical imagery; it does not supply the exemption, because the prophet has just said ye will revolt more and more.

Scripture holds both without strain. The sickness is real and the guilt is real, and the same chapter that diagnoses untended sores commands the nation to wash, to put away evil, to cease to do evil and learn to do well, and then promises that scarlet sins shall be as white as snow. The ointment and the repentance come together or not at all. A ministry that offers the soothing without the summons leaves the sore exactly where Isaiah found it.
roots_summary: Latin mollis, soft, plus facere, to make; Isaiah 1:6 names the ointment Judah's sores never received.
roots_lines: Latin mollificare, from mollis, soft, and facere, to make.

Luke 10:34 shows the Samaritan doing what Judah's shepherds would not.
